To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) technique can be used to detect microstructural abnormalities in the white matter of the brain.

(i) DTI can be used as a biomarker for the diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorders in first-degree relatives of patients; and (ii) that DTI can also be used as a potential biomarker to differentiate between schizophrenia and bipolar disorders.
The first degree relatives of patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder have a higher prevalence of psychotic disorders and schizophrenia spectrum disorders than the general population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new, efficient and environmentally benign processes and products.
the development of novel, efficient and robust algorithms for image segmentation and registration.
the development and validation of a new method for the determination of the diffusion tensor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence for the efficacy of antidepressants in the acute treatment of bipolar depression is strong and that antidepressants are a reasonable treatment choice for patients with bipolar I or bipolar II disorder.
the evidence for an association between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and a number of autoimmune and inflammatory disorders is weak.
the findings of the present study support the idea that schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are neurodevelopmental disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that there is an association between the presence of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in a family and the presence of a specific pattern of white matter abnormalities.
the results of this study suggest that the DTI measures of white matter integrity in first degree relatives may be a potential endophenotype for both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
the findings from our research group have provided support to the hypothesis that there are neurodevelopmental changes in schizophrenia, which are associated with the risk for developing the illness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is a dynamic organ and the changes that occur in the brain are not static but rather are dynamic and are changing over time.
we can use the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to detect the white matter abnormalities of schizophrenia and bipolar patients.
there are differences in the brain structure of people who have a family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder compared with those who don’t.
